assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Genome
items.clue: The entire genetic material of an organism.

items.label: Allele
items.clue: One of the different forms a gene may have.

items.label: DNA
items.clue: The chemical of which the genetic material in the nucleus of a cell is composed.

items.label: Phenotype
items.clue: The characteristics that the genotype develops and that are expressed in the organism.

questions.stem: DNA is a polymer. Which describes the repeating unit it is made from?

options.text: An amino acid joined to a sugar and phosphate group
A base joined directly on to the next base in the strand
Just one of the four different bases, A, C, G or T
A nucleotide of sugar, phosphate and one of four bases

questions.explanation: DNA is a polymer made from four different nucleotides; each nucleotide consists of a common sugar and phosphate group with one of four different bases attached to the sugar.

questions.stem: A mouse has two different alleles for fur colour. Which statement is correct?

options.text: It is homozygous, because two alleles are present here.
It is heterozygous, so the recessive allele is expressed.
It is heterozygous, so the dominant allele is shown.
It is heterozygous, so genotype equals phenotype.

questions.explanation: If the alleles are different the organism is heterozygous, and a dominant allele is always expressed even if only one copy is present.

questions.stem: Which alleles cause polydactyly and cystic fibrosis?

options.text: Polydactyly dominant; cystic fibrosis recessive
Both are dominant, as the disorders are common
Both are recessive, as one copy is enough here
Polydactyly recessive; cystic fibrosis is dominant

questions.explanation: Polydactyly (having extra fingers or toes) is caused by a dominant allele, and cystic fibrosis (a disorder of cell membranes) is caused by a recessive allele.

questions.stem: What do ordinary human body cells contain?

options.text: 23 pairs of chromosomes, one pair determining sex
23 chromosomes in total, one of them determining sex
23 pairs of chromosomes, with XY in every female
23 pairs of chromosomes, all from the mother's egg

questions.explanation: Ordinary human body cells contain 23 pairs of chromosomes: 22 pairs control characteristics only, but one of the pairs carries the genes that determine sex.

questions.stem: A coding section of DNA contains 30 bases. How many amino acids does this code for?

options.text: 10, because three bases code for one amino acid
30, because one base codes for one amino acid
15, because each pair of bases codes for one acid
1, because the section codes for a characteristic

questions.explanation: A sequence of three bases is the code for a particular amino acid, so 30 bases code for 10 amino acids.

questions.stem: A plant has the genotype Tt, where T is the dominant allele. What is its phenotype?

options.text: It shows T only if T is common in the population.
It shows the characteristic of the t allele only.
Its phenotype is written as the full genotype Tt.
It shows the characteristic of the T allele.

questions.explanation: A dominant allele is always expressed, even if only one copy is present, so the alleles present develop the characteristic coded by T.

questions.stem: A couple are offered embryo screening. Which of these is an ethical issue they might consider?

options.text: Whether one gene controls all the embryo's traits
Whether the screening test is medically accurate
Whether rejecting an embryo with an allele is right
Whether a gene codes for a trait or for a protein

questions.explanation: Embryo screening raises economic, social and ethical issues, and whether it is right to reject an embryo because of the alleles it carries is an ethical judgement.

questions.stem: A genetic cross is carried out between XX and XY parents. What does it predict about the offspring?

options.text: 1 female to 1 male, so a 50% chance of each
Exactly 2 girls and 2 boys in four babies
All female, as the egg cell decides sex
3 females to 1 male, as X is dominant here

questions.explanation: The cross gives XX, XX, XY and XY, a simple ratio of 1 female to 1 male, so there is a 50% probability of each sex.

questions.stem: What forms the two long strands of a DNA molecule?

options.text: Nucleotides made only of the four bases
Alternating sugar and phosphate sections
Four bases joined end to end in order
Amino acids joined end to end in chains

questions.explanation: The long strands of DNA consist of alternating sugar and phosphate sections, with one of the four bases attached to each sugar.

questions.stem: Two heterozygous mice (Bb) are crossed, where B is dominant. Which ratio of phenotypes does a Punnett square predict?

options.text: 3 with the dominant characteristic to 1 without
1 with the dominant characteristic to 3 without
4 with the dominant characteristic to 0 without
2 with the dominant characteristic and 2 without

questions.explanation: The Punnett square gives BB, Bb, Bb and bb. The dominant allele is expressed in the first three, so the predicted ratio is 3 to 1.

questions.stem: In a family tree, two parents who do not have cystic fibrosis have a child who does. What does this show?

options.text: The allele causing the disorder is dominant.
The parents' genotype matches their phenotype.
Each parent carries one recessive allele.
Only one parent carries the recessive allele.

questions.explanation: Cystic fibrosis is caused by a recessive allele, which is only expressed if two copies are present, so each unaffected parent must carry one copy to pass on.

questions.stem: A student uses a single gene cross to predict a person's height. Why is this prediction unreliable?

options.text: Every characteristic is controlled by one single gene here.
Most characteristics result from multiple genes interacting.
A gene codes directly for the characteristic, not protein.
A single cross gives exact numbers of offspring produced.

questions.explanation: Some characteristics are controlled by a single gene, but most characteristics are a result of multiple genes interacting rather than a single gene.

questions.stem: In the complementary strands of DNA, how are the bases linked?

options.text: A is linked to C, while G is linked to T
Every base links to the next base along
Each base links to a matching identical base
C is linked to G, and T is linked to A

questions.explanation: In the complementary strands a C is always linked to a G on the opposite strand and a T to an A.

questions.stem: In mice, black fur (B) is dominant to brown (b). A black mouse is crossed with a brown mouse and some brown offspring are produced. What was the black parent's genotype?

options.text: BB, since its two alleles are the same
bb, since a b allele was expressed here
Bb, since it passed on a b allele
BB, since B is the more common allele

questions.explanation: A brown offspring must be bb, so it received a b allele from each parent. The black parent expressed B but also carried b, so its genotype was Bb.

questions.stem: Where are proteins synthesised, and how do the amino acids reach the chain?

options.text: On ribosomes; carrier molecules bring the amino acids
On ribosomes; the DNA strand itself is the amino acids
In the cytoplasm's DNA; carrier molecules bring bases
In the nucleus; carrier molecules bring the amino acids

questions.explanation: Proteins are synthesised on ribosomes, according to a template, and carrier molecules bring specific amino acids to add to the growing protein chain in the correct order.

questions.stem: An enzyme is able to do its job because of which feature of the protein?

options.text: The characteristic that its gene codes for
The number of amino acids in its finished chain
The place in the nucleus where it was made
The unique shape it folds into at the end

questions.explanation: When the protein chain is complete it folds up to form a unique shape, and this unique shape enables proteins to do their job as enzymes, hormones or structures such as collagen.

questions.stem: Which statement about mutations is correct?

options.text: Each one alters the protein that is made.
Most do not alter the protein produced.
Only those in non-coding DNA have no effect.
Each one alters a characteristic directly.

questions.explanation: Mutations occur continuously, and most do not alter the protein, or only alter it slightly so that its appearance or function is not changed.

questions.stem: A mutation changes the shape of an enzyme. What is the likely effect?

options.text: The enzyme may no longer fit the substrate binding site.
Every other protein in the cell is altered in the same way.
There is no effect, because this DNA is non-coding DNA.
The enzyme still works, because only its length matters.

questions.explanation: A few mutations code for an altered protein with a different shape: an enzyme may no longer fit the substrate binding site, or a structural protein may lose its strength.
